case_study_insert.main_stem: Bluewater Cruises (BWC) is a cooperative in the tourism and leisure sector, employing a workforce of 95. Founded in 2007 by Sofia Marino, it operates river cruises on scenic routes through the valley and uses a flat structure with democratic leadership among its member-crew. BWC plans to invest $2,000,000 in a new passenger vessel, financed by member share subscriptions and a $1,200,000 ten-year bank loan. It has fixed costs of $2,700,000 a year, a variable cost of $270 per cruise berth and a selling price of $450 per cruise berth, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. BWC faces two problems: cabin-service complaints are rising and crew absenteeism has reached 11%, disrupting sailings.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Cabin Service and Guest Report, Q4 2025: BWC sailed 9,600 passenger-berths last quarter, with cabin-service complaint cards rising from 28 to 49 per month. The defect rate on cabin fittings reached 2.9% and deck-cleaning waste was 6.4% of supplies. Average boarding time was 35 minutes. A survey of 650 passengers found 70% would pay $25 more for a newer vessel and 57% rate cabin cleanliness as their top priority. Crew service training costs $520 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Bluewater Cruises as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for operators with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.40 to $13.17 per hour from April 2026. (3) Marine fuel and provisioning costs have risen 12.6% year-on-year, while cruise bookings grew 4.4% and inflation is 6.9%.

questions.question_text: BWC is funding its $2,000,000 vessel partly through member share subscriptions. Explain two advantages for BWC of this source of finance rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Member share subscriptions bring in ownership money that does not require interest or repayment, unlike the $1,200,000 bank loan whose cost rises with the base rate now at 5.0%. As a cooperative, BWC can draw on its member-crew and community, keeping more of the $180 contribution per berth to meet $2,700,000 fixed costs instead of paying a lender while marine fuel costs rise 12.6%; tackling the 49 cabin complaints also needs cash that interest would otherwise absorb.

Point 2: Member ownership strengthens commitment to the cooperative and gives members a voice in how the new vessel is run, which supports the flat structure and democratic leadership. It also avoids pledging BWC's $7,200,000 of non-current assets as collateral, so a downturn in the 4.4% growth of cruise bookings would not put the vessel at risk of repossession as it would with loan finance, and members are more likely to back a vessel they have helped fund.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to BWC's financing and cooperative structure.

questions.question_text: BWC wants to fill berths on its new vessel. Consider river-port leaflets, email campaigns to past passengers, or short video adverts on social media. Which should BWC choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
River-port leaflets: Leaflets handed out at ports are cheap and reach people already near the departure points. However, their reach is tiny compared with the 40,000 berths BWC must sell, they cannot show the new vessel, and response cannot be measured, which is a problem when the $2,000,000 vessel must be covered.

Email campaigns to past passengers: Emailing previous guests is low-cost and can offer repeat bookers the $450 berth directly, using the database behind 9,600 passenger-berths last quarter. It is measurable and personal. Its weakness is reach: it cannot attract the 70% of 650 surveyed passengers willing to pay $25 more for a newer vessel if they have never cruised with BWC, so it cannot expand demand much beyond 4.4% growth.

Short video adverts on social media: Video can show the newer vessel and the cleanliness that 57% of passengers rank first, reaching far beyond past guests at controlled cost, with click-through tracking. The risk is that views do not convert into bookings and constant content is needed, so early spend may be slow to pay back.

Recommendation: BWC should choose short video adverts on social media. They showcase the newer vessel to the 70% who would pay $25 more and the 57% who prioritise cleanliness, reaching new passengers that emails miss. Leaflets are rejected for negligible, unmeasurable reach and emails for failing to attract new cruisers; video gives the scale needed to fill 40,000 berths against the $1,200,000 loan, and the adverts can be changed quickly if the 4.4% booking growth stalls.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to BWC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in BWC's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in BWC's context with a justified recommendation explaining why leaflets and emails are rejected.

questions.question_text: BWC's cabin-service complaints have risen to 49 a month and absenteeism is 11%. Explain two benefits for BWC of its democratic leadership style.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 95 crew to suggest how to cut the 49 monthly cabin-service complaints, and because the structure is flat their ideas about boarding and cabin checks can be tried quickly. Member-crew who help set standards are more likely to meet the 57% of surveyed passengers who rank cleanliness first, protecting the 9,600 berths sailed last quarter; fewer complaints also protect the 70% who would pay $25 more for a newer vessel.

Point 2: Giving the crew a real voice raises commitment and can reduce the 11% absenteeism that disrupts cabin service and lengthens the 35-minute boarding time. Higher involvement also makes the $520-per-employee service training more effective, as members apply ideas themselves rather than obeying instructions, which suits a cooperative with shared ownership. The 9,600 berths sailed last quarter depend on reliable crews, so cutting 11% absence matters, and in a cooperative members have a direct stake in that reputation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to BWC's complaints, absence and crew.

questions.question_text: BWC must improve cabin service. Consider job enrichment or team working for the cabin crew. Which should BWC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Job enrichment: Giving each crew member responsibility for a whole cabin area, with a say in cleanliness checks, makes the work more meaningful and can raise the standards wanted by 57% of surveyed passengers. It suits the cooperative's democratic leadership and may reduce the 11% absenteeism. However, it depends on motivated individuals, takes time to design, and one weak member could leave the 49 monthly complaints unresolved on their section, although the 35-minute boarding time could improve if crew members take charge of their own area.

Team working: Organising cabin crews into teams with shared checklists lets members cover for the 11% absenteeism, standardise service across the vessel and jointly tackle the 49 complaints. Teams support the flat structure and allow experienced crew to coach newcomers on the new vessel, making the $520 training stick; teams can also rotate tasks when the 2.9% fitting defects create extra cleaning work. The risks are group conflict, slower decisions and blurred responsibility if no team leader is clear.

Decision: BWC should choose team working, adding elements of job enrichment within each team. Teams directly cover absences and raise consistent standards on the $2,000,000 vessel, while the 6.2% wage rise makes paid individual enrichment harder to afford. Job enrichment alone is rejected because it cannot shield service when 11% of crew are absent, whereas teams redistribute work and protect the 40,000-berth target. With $2,700,000 fixed costs to cover and 6.2% wage inflation, this is a low-cost way to raise standards. Stronger service also protects the 70% who would pay $25 more.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two approaches with limited application to BWC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in BWC's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches with a justified decision covering absence, standards and cost.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BWC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $2,700,000 ÷ ($450 − $270) = $2,700,000 ÷ $180 = 15,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 15,000 cruise berths a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $450 − $270 = $180. Answer: contribution per unit is $180.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BWC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. BWC can compare the 15,000-berth break-even with 40,000 berths sold, a margin of safety of 25,000, to see how far bookings can fall while the new vessel enters service.
2. The $180 contribution lets managers test the survey premium: if the 70% who would pay $25 more did so, contribution would be $205 and break-even $2,700,000 ÷ $205 = 13,171 berths, showing the value of a newer vessel.
3. Managers can use break-even to set the berth volume needed to cover $2,700,000 fixed costs and service the $1,200,000 loan before the cooperative commits more capital.
4. Average total cost of $2,700,000 ÷ 40,000 + $270 = $337.50 per berth can be benchmarked monthly to reveal the 12.6% fuel rise and guide the $520 crew training spend.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 15,000 berths | (ii) Contribution per unit = $180 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 40,000 berths; $25 vessel premium and break-even of 13,171; loan-service target; and average total cost of $337.50 to track 12.6% fuel inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BWC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has BWC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.34 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.36 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.91 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $240,000 trade receivables + $80,000 cash = $470,000; 2025 current assets = $130,000 + $300,000 + $60,000 = $490,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $470,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.34; 2025 = $490,000 ÷ $360,000 = 1.36. Excluding stock, 2024 = ($470,000 − $150,000) ÷ $350,000 = $320,000 ÷ $350,000 = 0.91; 2025 = ($490,000 − $130,000) ÷ $360,000 = $360,000 ÷ $360,000 = 1.00.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved modestly on both measures. Current assets rose from $470,000 to $490,000 while current liabilities increased only from $350,000 to $360,000, so short-term cover edged up. The stricter test improved from 0.91 to 1.00 because inventories fell from $150,000 to $130,000, meaning BWC no longer needs to rely on selling stores to meet near-term obligations. The concern is that cash fell from $80,000 to $60,000 while trade receivables climbed from $240,000 to $300,000, so much of the improvement is in invoices rather than money in the bank — risky with a $1,200,000 loan and $2,000,000 vessel planned.

Conclusion: BWC's financial position has improved, but only slightly and with a clear caveat. Both measures rose and the stricter measure no longer depends on inventory, yet rising receivables and lower cash mean the cooperative should tighten credit control before borrowing further for the new vessel. The $7,200,000 of non-current assets makes liquidity management important.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on BWC's financial position.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BWC of improving cabin-service quality on its cruises.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey found 57% of 650 passengers rank cabin cleanliness first and 70% would pay $25 more for a newer vessel, so better cabin service can justify a higher effective price and raise bookings. Cleaning up the 49 monthly complaints also supports the $450 berth price and the $180 contribution needed to fund the $2,000,000 vessel; 9,600 berths last quarter show the repeat business at stake.

Disadvantage: Better service needs more training at $520 per employee and may slow boarding, already 35 minutes, if checks are tightened, potentially adding to $2,700,000 fixed costs. With marine fuel up 12.6% and crew absenteeism at 11%, extra quality work may not be sustained, and the 2.9% fitting-defect rate would still generate complaints, while repairs may add to the $2,700,000 fixed costs. The $520 per-employee training must also be repeated if 11% absence continues. Better service also supports the 4.4% growth in cruise bookings the cooperative is targeting.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to BWC's survey, complaints and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 12.6% rise in marine fuel and provisioning costs will affect BWC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If BWC's $1,200,000 loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.75% × $1,200,000 = $9,000 a year, which is modest against $2,700,000 fixed costs; a fixed-rate loan would face no direct increase. Higher rates might slow the 4.4% growth in cruise bookings and raise the cost of the $2,000,000 vessel, but fixing the rate limits this risk.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.17 per hour): With a workforce of 95, crew wages rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours or individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented; the fair test is productivity — 40,000 berths ÷ 95 crew = about 421 berths per employee. If the new vessel raises berths sold, the $180 contribution can absorb the rise; if 11% absenteeism persists, unit labour costs rise instead.

Marine fuel and provisioning costs (+12.6%): These feed the $270 variable cost per berth. As a labelled upper bound, if all $270 rose 12.6% that is $34.02 per berth (12.6% × $270), or about $1,360,800 a year at 40,000 berths. Even a partial rise sharply cuts the $180 contribution, and the $25 premium wanted by 70% of passengers offsets only part of it while bookings grow 4.4%.

Conclusion: The 12.6% rise in fuel and provisioning will have the greatest impact. It applies to every berth, is much larger than the capped interest effect and the productivity-dependent wage effect, and directly threatens the $180 contribution that must cover $2,700,000 fixed costs and service the $1,200,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to BWC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BWC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in BWC's context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
